questions.prompt: A match is struck and burns in the air. Sort each item into the system (the matter that reacts and what it turns into) or the surroundings.

items.text: Chemicals in the match head
items.rationale: They react as soon as the match is struck, so they are part of the system.

items.text: Nitrogen in the nearby air, which does not react
items.rationale: It takes no part in the reaction, so it is surroundings; it simply warms up.

items.text: The wood that burns
items.rationale: The burning wood is a reactant, so it is inside the system.

items.text: Carbon dioxide and water vapor that form
items.rationale: Products are the same matter as the reactants, regrouped, so they stay in the system.

items.text: A metal tray under the match
items.rationale: The tray does not react; it is surroundings that can take in energy from the flame.

items.text: Oxygen from the air that reacts
items.rationale: This oxygen joins the reaction, so it counts as system even though it came from the air.

questions.explanation: The system is every bit of matter that takes part: the match-head chemicals, the wood and the oxygen that reacts, plus the ash, carbon dioxide and water vapor they become. questions.misconception: Only the starting substances count as the system, and anything that comes from the air, or forms later, is outside it.
questions.hint: For each item ask: does it take part in the reaction, either as a starting substance or as something that forms?

choices.text: The ammonium chloride as it dissolves
choices.rationale: This is the system itself, the substance whose change we are tracking.

choices.text: The skin of your arm under the pack
choices.rationale: Correct: your skin doesn't take part in the dissolving, so it is surroundings, and it loses energy to the pack.

choices.text: Ammonium chloride in a fresh pack touching it
choices.rationale: Correct: it is the same kind of substance, and it touches this pack, so it can trade energy with it. But it isn't the matter changing in this pack, so it is outside this system, part of the surroundings.

choices.text: The air around the pack
choices.rationale: Correct: the air doesn't take part in the dissolving, so it is surroundings that can give energy to the pack.

choices.text: The dissolved ammonium and chloride particles
choices.rationale: These are the ammonium chloride after it dissolves, the same matter, so they are still the system.

questions.explanation: The system is only the ammonium chloride changing in this pack, before and after it dissolves. Your skin and the air don't take part, so they are surroundings. So is the ammonium chloride in the fresh pack touching it: same kind of substance, but outside this boundary, and close enough to trade energy with the pack. Energy flows from your skin and the air into the system, which is why they cool.
questions.misconception: A substance stops being part of the system once it has changed, or any matter with the same name as the system must belong to it.
questions.hint: Which choices are the very matter changing in this pack, before or after it dissolves? Everything else is outside the boundary.

choices.text: The air just above the dish warms up

choices.text: The reaction gives off a bright glow

questions.accessiblePrompt: What is the net direction of energy transfer in an exothermic reaction?

choices.text: Both ways equally, so there is no net direction

questions.prompt: Match each single step or whole reaction to what it means for energy.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Match each single step or whole reaction to what it means for energy. The items are: breaking a bond between two atoms; forming a new bond between two atoms; a reaction whose new bonds give out more energy than breaking the old bonds took in; and a reaction whose bond breaking takes in more energy than its new bonds give out. The meanings are: whole reaction, the surroundings lose energy overall, endothermic; one step that gives energy out; whole reaction, the surroundings gain energy overall, exothermic; and one step that takes energy in.

left.text: Breaking a bond between two atoms
left.rationale: One step: pulling bonded atoms apart always costs energy, so breaking a bond takes energy in.

left.text: Forming a new bond between two atoms
left.rationale: One step: when atoms bond, energy is released, so forming a bond gives energy out.

left.text: A reaction whose new bonds give out more energy than breaking the old bonds took in
left.rationale: A whole reaction: its new bonds give out more than breaking the old ones took in, so the extra energy flows to the surroundings. That is exothermic.

left.text: A reaction whose bond breaking takes in more energy than its new bonds give out
left.rationale: A whole reaction: breaking its bonds takes in more than its new bonds give back, so the difference comes from the surroundings. That is endothermic.

right.text: One step that takes energy in
One step that gives energy out
Whole reaction: the surroundings gain energy overall (exothermic)
Whole reaction: the surroundings lose energy overall (endothermic)

questions.explanation: Pulling bonded atoms apart always costs energy, and forming a bond always releases energy; each is a single step. A typical reaction does both, so for the whole reaction you compare the totals. Extra energy the system gives out ends up in the surroundings, and extra energy it takes in comes from them. More released than absorbed means exothermic; more absorbed than released means endothermic.

questions.prompt: Switching to a thick bag that lets oxygen in slowly made a hand warmer last about 4 hours, but at only about 40 °C. What best explains the change?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Switching to a thick bag that lets oxygen in slowly made a hand warmer last about 4 hours, but at only about 40 degrees Celsius. What best explains the change?

choices.text: The iron reacted more slowly, spreading its energy over more time
choices.rationale: Correct: with oxygen arriving slowly, the same stored energy came out over hours instead of minutes, so the peak was lower.

choices.text: The thick bag changed the reaction from exothermic to endothermic
choices.rationale: The pack still stayed well above room temperature, so energy was still flowing out: it is still exothermic.

choices.text: Less energy came out in total, so the pack ran cooler
choices.rationale: The pack held the same iron and stayed warm for about 4 hours instead of under 1, so it didn't give out less energy. The same stored energy came out more slowly, which kept the peak lower.

choices.text: The thick bag trapped cold air that canceled some of the heat
choices.rationale: Cold isn't something that cancels heat. The lower peak came from energy being released more slowly.

questions.explanation: Iron needs oxygen to react. A bag that lets oxygen in slowly slows the reaction, so the same supply of stored energy comes out over hours instead of minutes. A lower peak doesn't mean less energy: temperature tells how hot the pack gets, not how much energy it gives out in total. Releasing energy more slowly gives a lower peak but a longer warm time: a trade-off.
questions.misconception: A lower peak temperature means less energy was released in total.
questions.hint: What does iron need from the air to react, and what happens if it arrives slowly?
